claim: Nitric oxide (NO) shows great potential for the treatment of many kinds of diseases as a gaseous therapeutic agent.
source: Nitric oxide (NO), as a gaseous therapeutic agent, shows great potential for the treatment of many kinds of diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about NO's therapeutic potential, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The immunogenicity and long-term toxicity of artificial carriers hinder the potential clinical translation of NO delivery systems.
source: Although various NO delivery systems have emerged, the immunogenicity and long-term toxicity of artificial carriers hinder the potential clinical translation of these gas therapeutics.
evidence: This statement identifies limitations of current NO delivery systems based on established challenges in the field.

claim: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have the capacities of self-renewal, differentiation, and low immunogenicity.
source: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), with the capacities of self-renewal, differentiation, and low immunogenicity, have been used as living carriers.
evidence: This describes well-established properties of MSCs cited in the scientific literature.

claim: MSCs as gaseous signaling molecule (GSM) carriers have not been reported prior to this study.
source: However, MSCs as gaseous signaling molecule (GSM) carriers have not been reported.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach based on literature review.

claim: Human MSCs were genetically modified to produce mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A) in this study.
source: In this study, human MSCs were genetically modified to produce mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: A new NO prodrug, 6-methyl-galactose-benzyl-oxy NONOate (MGP), was designed.
source: Furthermore, a new NO prodrug, 6-methyl-galactose-benzyl-oxy NONOate (MGP), was designed.
evidence: This describes the design of a novel compound in the study.

claim: MGP can enter cells and selectively trigger NO release from genetically engineered MSCs (eMSCs) in the presence of β-GALH363A.
source: MGP can enter cells and selectively trigger NO release from genetically engineered MSCs (eMSCs) in the presence of β-GALH363A.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of action demonstrated in the study.

claim: eMSCs can release NO when MGP is systemically administered in a mouse model of acute kidney injury (AKI).
source: Moreover, our results revealed that eMSCs can release NO when MGP is systemically administered in a mouse model of acute kidney injury (AKI), which can achieve NO release in a precise spatiotemporal manner and augment the therapeutic efficiency of MSCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo experiments conducted in the study.

claim: The eMSC and NO prodrug system can achieve NO release in a precise spatiotemporal manner.
source: Moreover, our results revealed that eMSCs can release NO when MGP is systemically administered in a mouse model of acute kidney injury (AKI), which can achieve NO release in a precise spatiotemporal manner and augment the therapeutic efficiency of MSCs.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the system demonstrated in the study.

claim: The eMSC and NO prodrug system augments the therapeutic efficiency of MSCs.
source: Moreover, our results revealed that eMSCs can release NO when MGP is systemically administered in a mouse model of acute kidney injury (AKI), which can achieve NO release in a precise spatiotemporal manner and augment the therapeutic efficiency of MSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in the AKI model.

claim: NO plays vital roles in various physiological processes, including tissue regeneration.
source: Nitric oxide (NO), as a gaseous signaling molecule (GSM), plays vital roles in various physiological processes, including tissue regeneration (Midgley et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NO has an extremely short half-life.
source: Due to the extremely short half-life of NO, efforts to extensively enhance the therapeutic efficacy of NO by various types of artificial carriers, such as polymers, peptides, and nanoparticles, have achieved many successes, and there are remaining challenges that need to be addressed, including off-targeting, toxicity, immunogenicity, and clinical translation (Wilhelm et al., 2016; Park, 2013).
evidence: This is a well-known property of NO cited in the literature.

claim: Various types of artificial carriers for NO delivery include polymers, peptides, and nanoparticles.
source: Due to the extremely short half-life of NO, efforts to extensively enhance the therapeutic efficacy of NO by various types of artificial carriers, such as polymers, peptides, and nanoparticles, have achieved many successes, and there are remaining challenges that need to be addressed, including off-targeting, toxicity, immunogenicity, and clinical translation (Wilhelm et al., 2016; Park, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Remaining challenges for NO delivery systems include off-targeting, toxicity, immunogenicity, and clinical translation.
source: Due to the extremely short half-life of NO, efforts to extensively enhance the therapeutic efficacy of NO by various types of artificial carriers, such as polymers, peptides, and nanoparticles, have achieved many successes, and there are remaining challenges that need to be addressed, including off-targeting, toxicity, immunogenicity, and clinical translation (Wilhelm et al., 2016; Park, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Successful NO delivery requires an appropriate carrier for delivering therapeutic molecules to target sites in an on-demand and controlled manner.
source: Successful NO delivery requires an appropriate carrier for delivering these therapeutic molecules to the target sites in an on-demand and controlled manner, as well as in a protected, pharmacologically active form (Weaver et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Bioinspired delivery vehicles include biological cells, exosomes, and isolated membrane ghosts.
source: Bioinspired delivery vehicles, including biological cells, exosomes, and isolated membrane ghosts, are highly attractive because they exhibit excellent biodistribution, immune compatibility, innate disease-targeting abilities, and reduced toxicity (Bush et al., 2021; Yoo et al., 2011; Samanta et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bioinspired delivery vehicles exhibit excellent biodistribution, immune compatibility, innate disease-targeting abilities, and reduced toxicity.
source: Bioinspired delivery vehicles, including biological cells, exosomes, and isolated membrane ghosts, are highly attractive because they exhibit excellent biodistribution, immune compatibility, innate disease-targeting abilities, and reduced toxicity (Bush et al., 2021; Yoo et al., 2011; Samanta et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MSCs have gained considerable attention as drug-delivery vehicles owing to their genetic tractability, payload diversity, intrinsic tropism for disease sites, and differentiation potential.
source: Among these systems, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have gained considerable attention as drug-delivery vehicles owing to their genetic tractability, payload diversity, intrinsic tropism for disease sites, and differentiation potential (Tran and Damaser, 2015; Thanuja et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MSCs are adult stem cells capable of self-renewal and multilineage differentiation.
source: MSCs are adult stem cells capable of self-renewal and multilineage differentiation that have been reported to promote tissue regeneration mediated by immunomodulatory and proangiogenic properties via paracrine effects, and MSC-based cell therapeutics have entered multiple clinical trials (Baraniak and McDevitt, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MSCs promote tissue regeneration mediated by immunomodulatory and proangiogenic properties via paracrine effects.
source: MSCs are adult stem cells capable of self-renewal and multilineage differentiation that have been reported to promote tissue regeneration mediated by immunomodulatory and proangiogenic properties via paracrine effects, and MSC-based cell therapeutics have entered multiple clinical trials (Baraniak and McDevitt, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MSC-based cell therapeutics have entered multiple clinical trials.
source: MSCs are adult stem cells capable of self-renewal and multilineage differentiation that have been reported to promote tissue regeneration mediated by immunomodulatory and proangiogenic properties via paracrine effects, and MSC-based cell therapeutics have entered multiple clinical trials (Baraniak and McDevitt, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MSCs do not express blood-group antigens or MHC class II antigens.
source: Previous studies revealed that MSCs do not express blood-group antigens or MHC class II antigens and have long been reported to be hypoimmunogenic or immune privileged, which possess the clinical potential of MSC-based cell therapy (Zhou and Shi, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MSCs have been reported to be hypoimmunogenic or immune privileged.
source: Previous studies revealed that MSCs do not express blood-group antigens or MHC class II antigens and have long been reported to be hypoimmunogenic or immune privileged, which possess the clinical potential of MSC-based cell therapy (Zhou and Shi, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MSCs as delivery vehicles have been widely studied for the delivery of peptides, proteins, DNA, and RNA.
source: MSCs as delivery vehicles have been widely studied for the delivery of various drugs and bioactive molecules into target disease sites, including peptides, proteins, DNA, and RNA (Peng et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The concept of MSCs as vehicles to deliver GSMs has not been studied prior to this work.
source: However, the concept of MSCs as vehicles to deliver GSMs has not been studied.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach based on literature review.

claim: Enzyme prodrug therapy is a versatile and exploitable technique to convert inactive, nontoxic prodrugs to active drugs at the desired sites.
source: To achieve a gas-generating platform based on living cells, MSCs are programmed to sustain the generation and release NO by taking advantage of enzyme prodrug therapy, a versatile and exploitable technique to convert inactive, nontoxic prodrugs to active drugs at the desired sites (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The expression of mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A) by eMSCs enabled the production of NO when the NO prodrug was administered.
source: In this advanced delivery platform, the expression of mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A) by eMSCs enabled the production of NO when the NO prodrug was administered.
evidence: This describes the mechanism demonstrated in the study.

claim: eMSCs could successfully generate and release NO in a precise spatiotemporal manner.
source: We hypothesized that eMSCs could successfully generate and release NO in a precise spatiotemporal manner, as well as augment the therapeutic effects of MSCs and result in superior efficacy of stem cell therapy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested in the study.

claim: eMSCs could augment the therapeutic effects of MSCs and result in superior efficacy of stem cell therapy.
source: We hypothesized that eMSCs could successfully generate and release NO in a precise spatiotemporal manner, as well as augment the therapeutic effects of MSCs and result in superior efficacy of stem cell therapy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested in the study.

claim: MSCs in this study represent human placenta-derived MSCs unless otherwise mentioned.
source: Other than mentioned in context, MSCs represent human placenta-derived MSCs.
evidence: This is a clarification about the cell type used in the study.

claim: MSCs were genetically modified to produce mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A) which triggers NO release from MSCs when the corresponding NO prodrug is applied.
source: To establish a living cell-mediated gas generation platform, MSCs were genetically modified to produce mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A), which triggers NO release from MSCs when the corresponding NO prodrug is applied and avoids the interference of endogenous glycosidase.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and mechanism.

claim: The use of mutant β-GALH363A avoids the interference of endogenous glycosidase.
source: To establish a living cell-mediated gas generation platform, MSCs were genetically modified to produce mutant β-galactosidase (β-GALH363A), which triggers NO release from MSCs when the corresponding NO prodrug is applied and avoids the interference of endogenous glycosidase.
evidence: This explains a design feature of the system.

claim: The expression of β-GALH363A in eMSCs was confirmed.
source: The expression of β-GALH363A in eMSCs was confirmed (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Rluc expression was confirmed by in vitro molecular imaging.
source: Moreover, Rluc expression was confirmed by in vitro molecular imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: eMSCs did not exhibit significant differences in morphology or MSC surface markers compared with wild-type MSCs.
source: Furthermore, compared with wild-type MSCs, eMSCs did not exhibit significant differences in morphology or MSC surface markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: MGP contains a lipid-soluble self-decomposition chain that enhances its water distribution coefficient and enables it to cross the cell membrane of eMSCs.
source: MGP contains a lipid-soluble self-decomposition chain oil that enhances its water distribution coefficient and enables it to cross the cell membrane of eMSCs and then be catalyzed by β-GALH363A to release NO from eMSCs.
evidence: This describes the design rationale for the prodrug.

claim: MGP can be specifically catalyzed by β-GALH363A and has sustained NO release behavior.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, MGP can be specifically catalyzed by β-GALH363A and has sustained NO release behavior.
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: MGP can diffuse into eMSCs and release NO.
source: We detected NO production in the medium of eMSCs with MGP administration using the Griess method, confirming that MGP can diffuse into eMSCs and release NO (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The characteristic triplet EPR signal was observed in eMSCs with MGP administration.
source: The characteristic triplet EPR signal was observed in eMSCs with MGP administration (Figure 1G), and we further confirmed that 1×106 eMSCs could release 1 nmol NO (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: 1×106 eMSCs could release 1 nmol NO.
source: The characteristic triplet EPR signal was observed in eMSCs with MGP administration (Figure 1G), and we further confirmed that 1×106 eMSCs could release 1 nmol NO (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: eMSCs could specifically release NO as visualized by DAF-FM diacetate staining.
source: Moreover, NO production of eMSCs with MGP administration was visualized by using diaminofluorescein (DAF)-FM diacetate, a cell-permeable fluorescent probe for the detection of intracellular NO, which also supported that eMSCs could specifically release NO (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The optimum concentration of MGP was 2 µg/mL based on cell viability, Ki67 immunostaining, and expression of proliferation-related genes.
source: Considering the cell-protective effects of a low NO concentration, our results revealed that the optimum concentration of MGP was 2 µg/mL by cell viability, immunostaining for the proliferation marker Ki67, and immunostaining for the expression of proliferation-related genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is determined by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: eMSC proliferation was markedly ameliorated by H2O2-induced oxidative stress as shown by BLI assay.
source: The bioluminescence imaging (BLI) assay showed that eMSC proliferation was markedly ameliorated by H2O2-induced oxidative stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A total of 228 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, of which 116 were upregulated genes and 112 were downregulated genes.
source: We identified a total of 228 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), of which 116 were upregulated genes and 112 were downregulated genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is from RNA-seq analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis showed enrichment in biological processes including protein transport, cell differentiation, morphogenesis, and oxidation-reduction processes.
source: Analysis of Gene Ontology (GO) categories was mainly enriched in biological processes, including protein transport, cell differentiation, morphogenesis, and oxidation-reduction processes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is from GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claim: NO may improve intracellular antioxidant capacity as suggested by GSEA.
source: Among them, the oxidation-reduction process attracted our attention, suggesting that NO may improve intracellular antioxidant capacity, which was confirmed by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from GSEA analysis shown in the figures.

claim: A significant increase in DEGs associated with antioxidation (GSR, SRXN1, RRBP1, BMI1, RPL24P4, and MAFG) was observed in eMSCs with MGP administration.
source: Meanwhile, we noted that a significant increase in some of the DEGs associated with antioxidation was observed in eMSCs with MGP administration, namely, GSR, SRXN1, RRBP1, BMI1, RPL24P4, and MAFG, indicating that NO may indeed play a cytoprotective role in eMSCs by elevating antioxidation capacity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is from RNA-seq data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: NO may play a cytoprotective role in eMSCs by elevating antioxidation capacity.
source: Meanwhile, we noted that a significant increase in some of the DEGs associated with antioxidation was observed in eMSCs with MGP administration, namely, GSR, SRXN1, RRBP1, BMI1, RPL24P4, and MAFG, indicating that NO may indeed play a cytoprotective role in eMSCs by elevating antioxidation capacity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data.

claim: NO led to robust increases in survival- or proliferation-related genes, including FER, NRSN2, UCK2, CAB39, SNHG4, and SYDE1.
source: We also found that NO led to robust increases in survival- or proliferation-related genes, including FER, NRSN2, UCK2, CAB39, SNHG4, and SYDE1 (Figure 2D), as well as angiogenesis-related genes, such as ARRB2, RHOQ, MYADM, and CFHR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is from RNA-seq data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: NO led to increases in angiogenesis-related genes, such as ARRB2, RHOQ, MYADM, and CFHR1.
source: We also found that NO led to robust increases in survival- or proliferation-related genes, including FER, NRSN2, UCK2, CAB39, SNHG4, and SYDE1 (Figure 2D), as well as angiogenesis-related genes, such as ARRB2, RHOQ, MYADM, and CFHR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is from RNA-seq data analysis shown in the figure.

claim: GSEA revealed negative regulation of cell apoptosis and positive regulation of angiogenesis by NO.
source: Consistent with the aforementioned findings, GSEA of the whole transcriptome also revealed negative regulation of cell apoptosis and positive regulation of angiogenesis by NO (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is from GSEA analysis shown in the figures.

claim: KEGG analysis highlighted pathways including the Jak-STAT signaling pathway and MAPK signaling pathway that may contribute to enhanced antioxidant capacity.
source: In addition, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis highlighted pathways that may contribute to enhanced antioxidant capacity, including the Jak-STAT signaling pathway and MAPK signaling pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is from KEGG pathway analysis shown in the figure.

claim: NO might be able to ameliorate the oxidative stress of eMSCs and inhibit cell apoptosis.
source: Together, these results demonstrated that NO might be able to ameliorate the oxidative stress of eMSCs and inhibit cell apoptosis (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and pathway analysis data.

claim: eMSCs with MGP administration exhibited increased cell retention and prolonged cell survival compared with the eMSC group in I/R-injured kidneys.
source: Although all groups gradually experienced donor cell death in the following days, eMSCs with MGP administration strikingly exhibited increased cell retention and prolonged cell survival in comparison with the eMSC group (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from BLI analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: eMSCs treated with MGP displayed higher cell proliferation and cell retention on day 3 as confirmed by immunohistology.
source: Furthermore, immunohistology also confirmed that the eMSCs with MGP administration displayed higher cell proliferation and cell retention on day 3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is from immunohistology data shown in the figure.

claim: eMSCs treated with MGP showed significantly lower levels of SCr and BUN.
source: Moreover, we found that the eMSCs treated with MGP showed significantly lower levels of SCr and BUN (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is from renal function measurements shown in the figures.

claim: Tubular dilation, cast formation, and massive loss of brush borders at the initial stage after injury (3 days) were obviously reduced after NO-eMSC system treatment.
source: Further kidney histology examination showed that tubular dilation, cast formation, and massive loss of brush borders at the initial stage after injury (3 days) were obviously reduced after NO-eMSC system treatment (Figure 3F to H).
evidence: This is from histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The development of interstitial fibrosis was consistent with the mRNA expression of ECM synthesis- and fibrosis pathway-related genes.
source: Kidney fibrosis analysis demonstrated that the development of interstitial fibrosis was consistent with the mRNA expression of ECM synthesis- and fibrosis pathway-related genes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is from fibrosis analysis and gene expression data shown in the figure.

claim: The expression of KIM-1 was significantly decreased in the proximal tubules of the kidneys in the eMSC with MGP administration group compared to the eMSC group.
source: Furthermore, the expression of KIM-1, a kidney injury marker, was significantly decreased in the proximal tubules of the kidneys in the eMSC with MGP administration group compared to the eMSC group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is from immunohistochemical staining data shown in the figure.

claim: The level of caspase-3/cleaved caspase-3 exhibited an abrupt increase in the injured kidney of the PBS group but was attenuated by eMSCs with MGP administration.
source: Simultaneously, we found that the level of caspase-3/cleaved caspase-3 exhibited an abrupt increase in the injured kidney of the PBS group but was attenuated by eMSCs with MGP administration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that the NO-eMSC system has protective effects on apoptosis in tubular epithelial cells.
evidence: This is from immunostaining data shown in the figure.

claim: The NO-eMSC system has protective effects on apoptosis in tubular epithelial cells.
source: Simultaneously, we found that the level of caspase-3/cleaved caspase-3 exhibited an abrupt increase in the injured kidney of the PBS group but was attenuated by eMSCs with MGP administration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that the NO-eMSC system has protective effects on apoptosis in tubular epithelial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the caspase-3 data.

claim: The NO-eMSC system could increase eMSC survival in vivo and further improve kidney function.
source: Overall, these results indicated that the NO-eMSC system could increase eMSC survival in vivo and further improve kidney function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experimental results.

claim: The NO level from eMSC-treated kidneys was significantly increased when the prodrug MGP was applied as shown by Griess and chemiluminescence assays.
source: The results from Griess (Figure 5A) and chemiluminescence assays (Figure 5B and C) showed that the NO level from eMSC-treated kidneys was significantly increased when the prodrug MGP was applied.
evidence: This is from NO measurement data shown in the figures.

claim: An obvious characteristic triplet EPR signal (NO signal) was observed in the eMSCs treated with MGP.
source: The EPR signal of NO was observed in all groups, while an obvious characteristic triplet EPR signal (NO signal) was observed in the eMSCs treated with MGP (Figure 5D and E), which further confirmed that eMSCs could release NO in vivo.
evidence: This is from EPR measurement data shown in the figures.

claim: eMSCs could release NO in vivo as confirmed by EPR.
source: The EPR signal of NO was observed in all groups, while an obvious characteristic triplet EPR signal (NO signal) was observed in the eMSCs treated with MGP (Figure 5D and E), which further confirmed that eMSCs could release NO in vivo.
evidence: This is from EPR measurement data shown in the figures.

claim: NO production from the kidney was significantly higher than that from the heart and liver.
source: The quantitative data showed that NO production from the kidney was significantly higher than that from the heart and liver (Figure 5F to H), suggesting that eMSCs could release NO specifically in the kidney.
evidence: This is from NO measurement data in different tissues shown in the figures.

claim: eMSCs could release NO specifically in the kidney.
source: The quantitative data showed that NO production from the kidney was significantly higher than that from the heart and liver (Figure 5F to H), suggesting that eMSCs could release NO specifically in the kidney.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific NO measurement data.

claim: The characteristic triplet EPR signal was observed in eAD-MSCs and ehUC-MSCs with MGP administration.
source: The characteristic triplet EPR signal was observed in eAD-MSCs and ehUC-MSCs with MGP administration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B), which was further confirmed by the Griess method (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is from EPR and Griess assay data shown in the figures.

claim: The eAD-MSCs and ehUC-MSCs treated with MGP showed significantly lower levels of SCr and BUN.
source: We found that the eAD-MSCs and ehUC-MSCs treated with MGP showed significantly lower levels of SCr and BUN (Figure 5—figure supplements 1E and 2E).
evidence: This is from renal function measurements shown in the figures.

claim: The expression of KIM-1 was significantly decreased in the proximal tubules of the kidneys in the eAD-MSC and ehUC-MSC with MGP administration groups.
source: Furthermore, the expression of KIM-1 (kidney injury marker) was significantly decreased in the proximal tubules of the kidneys in the eAD-MSC and ehUC-MSC with MGP administration groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is from immunostaining data shown in the figure.

claim: The MSC and NO prodrug system provides a tunable platform for NO delivery and holds promise for regenerative therapy.
source: Thus, our MSC and NO prodrug system provides a tunable platform for NO delivery and holds promise for regenerative therapy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with different MSC types.

claim: The NO-eMSC system could stimulate renal angiogenesis by activating the VEGF/VEGFR2 pathway.
source: According to the results of angiogenesis imaging, BLI signals were emitted in all groups, and the strongest signal was detected in the eMSCs with MGP administration group, which suggests that the NO-eMSC system could stimulate renal angiogenesis by activating the VEGF/VEGFR2 pathway (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from BLI data in VEGFR2-Fluc transgenic mice shown in the figures.

claim: CD31 immunostaining revealed significantly enhanced CD31+ microvascular density in the group of eMSCs with MGP administration.
source: The CD31 immunostaining results revealed significantly enhanced CD31+ microvascular density in the group of eMSCs with MGP administration, which is consistent with the BLI results (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is from immunostaining data shown in the figure.

claim: The eMSCs with MGP administration facilitated renal angiogenesis by upregulating angiogenic factor expression (VEGFR2, bFGF, PLGF, Ang-1, and Ang-2).
source: Moreover, the expression of the angiogenesis-related genes VEGFR2, bFGF, PLGF, Ang-1, and Ang-2 detected by real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) also confirmed that the eMSCs with MGP administration facilitated renal angiogenesis by upregulating angiogenic factor expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is from RT-PCR data shown in the figure.

claim: The numbers of proliferating Ki-67+ tubular cells were largely stimulated in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP.
source: As shown in Figure 6E and F, the numbers of proliferating Ki-67+ tubular cells were largely stimulated in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP, suggesting that the NO-eMSC system promoted kidney regeneration by accelerating tubular cell proliferation.
evidence: This is from immunostaining data shown in the figures.

claim: The NO-eMSC system promoted kidney regeneration by accelerating tubular cell proliferation.
source: As shown in Figure 6E and F, the numbers of proliferating Ki-67+ tubular cells were largely stimulated in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP, suggesting that the NO-eMSC system promoted kidney regeneration by accelerating tubular cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the Ki-67 staining data.

claim: eMSCs boosted the migration ability of HUVECs in a coculture system as evidenced by a scratch wound-healing assay.
source: Subsequently, we explored the mechanism of eMSCs with MGP administration-induced angiogenesis, and our data revealed that eMSCs boosted the migration ability of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) in a coculture system with Transwells, as evidenced by a scratch wound-healing assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is from wound-healing assay data shown in the figure.

claim: The angiogenic ability of HUVECs was visibly increased in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP as assessed by a tube formation assay.
source: Additionally, the angiogenic ability of HUVECs, as manifested by the number of nodes and branches, was visibly increased in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP, as assessed by a tube formation assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C, D, and E).
evidence: This is from tube formation assay data shown in the figures.

claim: eMSCs could inhibit the apoptosis of HUVECs as suggested by cleaved caspase-3 immunofluorescence staining.
source: Additionally, the protein level of cleaved caspase-3, a key apoptosis molecule, was detected by immunofluorescence staining, suggesting that eMSCs could inhibit the apoptosis of HUVECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is inferred from immunofluorescence staining data shown in the figure.

claim: eMSCs with MGP administration exert superior promotive effects on kidney angiogenesis after injury by enhancing the proangiogenic activities of vascular endothelial cells.
source: In general, we proposed that eMSCs with MGP administration exert superior promotive effects on kidney angiogenesis after injury by enhancing the proangiogenic activities of vascular endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the angiogenesis experiments.

claim: eMSCs with MGP administration increased the number of F4/80- and CD206-positive macrophages while decreasing the number of F4/80- and iNOS-positive macrophages.
source: We next explored the modulatory effect of eMSCs on the inflammatory response in I/R-injured kidneys, and our results showed that eMSCs with MGP administration increased the number of F4/80- and CD206-positive macrophages while decreasing the number of F4/80- and iNOS-positive macrophages, indicating that the NO-eMSC system could promote the polarization of M1 macrophages to M2 macrophages (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is from immunofluorescence staining data shown in the figures.

claim: The NO-eMSC system could promote the polarization of M1 macrophages to M2 macrophages.
source: We next explored the modulatory effect of eMSCs on the inflammatory response in I/R-injured kidneys, and our results showed that eMSCs with MGP administration increased the number of F4/80- and CD206-positive macrophages while decreasing the number of F4/80- and iNOS-positive macrophages, indicating that the NO-eMSC system could promote the polarization of M1 macrophages to M2 macrophages (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the macrophage marker staining data.

claim: mRNA expression profiling confirmed the polarization of M1 macrophages to M2 macrophages.
source: Meanwhile, mRNA expression profiling further confirmed this finding (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is from RT-PCR data shown in the figures.

claim: Oxidative stress-induced ROS are the main cause of renal I/R injury, leading to augmented inflammation and extended tissue damage.
source: Oxidative stress-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) are well known as the main cause of renal I/R injury, leading to subsequent augmented inflammation and extended tissue damage (Collard and Gelman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The eMSCs with MGP administration significantly decreased lipid deposition in renal tubules after I/R injury.
source: Excessive intracellular accumulation of lipids was observed in the renal tubules of the PBS group after I/R injury, while the eMSCs with MGP administration significantly decreased lipid deposition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is from Oil Red O staining data shown in the figure.

claim: The renal level of MDA was notably increased in the PBS group and significantly decreased in the eMSCs with MGP administration group.
source: Meanwhile, the renal level of MDA, an index of ROS-mediated lipid peroxidation, was notably increased in the PBS group and significantly decreased in the eMSCs with MGP administration group (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is from MDA measurement data shown in the figure.

claim: Remarkable upregulation of SOD and GSH levels was observed in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP.
source: Moreover, we examined the antioxidant capacity levels (SOD and GSH contents) in kidney tissues, and remarkable upregulation of SOD and GSH levels was observed in the group of eMSCs treated with MGP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is from SOD and GSH measurement data shown in the figures.

claim: The NO-eMSC system exhibited a renoprotective effect by targeting antioxidation and macrophage polarization-mediated anti-inflammation.

claim: Low levels of NO (nmol to μmol) are frequently associated with cell protection, while high concentrations (>mmol) of NO exert apoptotic effects.
source: Notably, the therapeutic effects of GSMs are highly concentration dependent; for example, low levels of NO (nmol to μmol) are frequently associated with cell protection, while high concentrations (>mmol) of NO exert apoptotic effects (Midgley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The insufficient solubility, poor stability, and unfavorable pharmacokinetics of GSM donors have prevented their wide application.
source: Although a plethora of GSM small molecule donors have been developed, the insufficient solubility, poor stability, and unfavorable pharmacokinetics of these GSM donors have prevented their wide application (Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NO is the first and most well-known gaseous molecule that plays critical roles in a wide spectrum of physiological and pathological processes.
source: NO, the first and most well-known gaseous molecule, has been widely shown to play critical roles in a wide spectrum of physiological and pathological processes (Hu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It remains a challenge to maintain long-term NO release and eliminate immunogenicity and systemic toxicity in NO delivery systems.
source: Although endogenous (enzyme and pH variations) or exogenous (light and ultrasound)-triggered NO delivery systems for controlled NO release profiles have been developed, it remains a challenge to maintain long-term NO release and eliminate immunogenicity and systemic toxicity (Zafonte et al., 2022; Shimizu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An increasing number of cell delivery systems have entered multiple clinical trials or been approved for marketing.

claim: Genetic engineering of MSCs is an approach to produce and deliver specific therapeutic proteins or enhance innate properties for treating diseases.
source: Genetic engineering of MSCs is an approach to produce and deliver specific therapeutic proteins or enhance innate properties such as migration, differentiation, and survival for treating many tremendous diseases (Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Genetically engineered MSCs offer long-term and stable production of the therapeutic protein of interest.
source: Therefore, genetically eMSCs, usually as living 'drug reservoirs', offer long-term and stable production of the therapeutic protein of interest and thus have gained appreciable attention as therapeutic delivery vehicles (Bush et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: NO dosing is controlled by the concentration of the administered NO prodrug.
source: NO dosing is controlled by the concentration of the administered NO prodrug, and an elevated NO signal was observed only at the site of transplanted eMSCs.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the system.

claim: The combinational use of NO-releasing biomaterials and stem cells is an emerging field of regenerative medicine.

claim: The eMSC-based NO delivery system can serve as a generic delivery system that holds promise for extensively broadening other gaseous molecule therapies.
source: In conclusion, we have developed a genetic eMSC-based NO delivery, NO-eMSC system, for targeted, controlled, and long-term NO delivery for the first time. This advanced NO delivery system can serve as a generic delivery system that holds promise for extensively broadening other gaseous molecule therapies and provides a new library of clinical solutions for regenerative medicine.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential applications of the system.
